title: Year four close: the house of many rooms
hook: the Catechism, Aquinas, the orders, justice, Mary and the East: rooms in one house
tomorrow: Year five opens: reading for yourself

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catholics disagree, from Paul and Peter at Antioch to Sunday lunch. Your line was unity, not sameness. Did you name what you share before where you differ? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-six.

A supper table at night, and friends who have just heard their teacher say he is going away. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells them not to let their hearts be troubled, and the picture he gives them is a house. In the Douay-Rheims: "In my Father's house there are many mansions." Mansions here means dwelling places, rooms to live in, and the next words speak of a place prepared for them. It's a promise about heaven. It's also a fair picture of what this year has been: a walk through one house, opening door after door, and finding each room lived in. Today, the year four close.
screen: `SUPPER, THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `MANY MANSIONS.` → `ONE HOUSE, MANY DOORS.`

segments.voice: Walk back through the house. The first room was the Catechism, read part by part: what Catholics believe, how they celebrate, how they live, and how they pray. That room is the floor plan; every other room sits on it. The next room was a study, with Thomas Aquinas at the desk, asking a question, listing the objections fairly, and answering with patience. Then a long hallway of religious orders. Benedictines, with their rule of prayer and work. Franciscans, with poverty and joy. Dominicans, preaching truth. Jesuits, finding God in all things. Carmelites, climbing into silent prayer. Each order is a different room for the same Gospel. Then the room that opens onto the street: Catholic social teaching, the dignity of every person, the common good, a preference for the poor. Then a quieter room, with Mary: her feasts, her titles, and what the Church teaches about her. Then a door some Catholics in the West rarely open, into the Eastern Catholic churches, with their own liturgies and icons, in full communion with Rome. And finally the devotions, the callings, and the neighbors: the rosary on a kitchen table, the vocation of a married couple or a hermit, a greeting sent to Muslim, Jewish and Hindu friends. Yesterday's lesson was that Catholics disagree. Today's is where they disagree: inside one house. A Benedictine and a Jesuit pray in different rooms, under one roof, at one table. That's what a house with many rooms is. Not a hotel of strangers. A family home, with doors open between the rooms.
screen: `THE CATECHISM IS THE FLOOR PLAN.` · `A STUDY, AND A HALLWAY OF ORDERS.` · `JUSTICE, MARY, AND THE EAST.` · `DEVOTIONS, CALLINGS, NEIGHBORS.` · then, large: `IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE THERE ARE MANY MANSIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose the room you'll live in most. Settle, and breathe. Walk slowly back through the year in your mind. The Catechism. Aquinas's study. The orders. Social justice. Mary. The East. The devotions and the callings. Notice which door you keep coming back to. Don't choose the room you think you should like. Choose the one that's already yours. Then picture one small thing you'll do this week to live in it. If you pray, you can thank God for that room. The bell holds the time.
Year four close. A year of schools of prayer and thought, walked like the rooms of one house, from the Catechism to the neighbors at the door. Today's word.
Your line: a house with many rooms. Today, spend ten minutes in the room you chose: a page, a prayer, an act of service. And tomorrow, year five opens. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics live their faith through different schools of prayer and thought within one Church: some are drawn to a religious order's spirituality, some to social justice, some to Marian devotion or the Eastern liturgies, all sharing the same creed and sacraments.

original.note: Greek: many dwelling places, in John 14:2, rendered many mansions in the Douay-Rheims.

trapdoor: what you thought: many mansions means big houses in heaven.
what it means: dwelling places, rooms in one Father's house, a promise Jesus made at supper with his friends.
what a scholar hears: the year's schools, the Catechism, Aquinas, the orders, justice, Mary and the East, as rooms under one roof.

notes: Douay-Rheims John 14:2: 'In my Father's house there are many mansions. If not, I would have told you: because I go to prepare a place for you.' Only the first sentence is quoted. Confirm.
The setting (supper on the night before he died, John 13–14) and 'mansions means dwelling places' are stated; the Greek μοναί (dwelling places) supports this. Confirm the gloss and the Greek accents.

The recap follows the year-four outline blocks: Catechism part by part; Aquinas; Benedictines, Franciscans, Dominicans, Jesuits, Carmelites; social teaching; Mary; Eastern Catholic churches; devotions; vocations and neighbors. One-line summaries of each order (prayer and work, poverty and joy, preaching truth, finding God in all things, silent prayer) are brief characterizations; confirm they match what those days taught.
The year-four days themselves were not all re-read for this recap; the recap avoids counts and dates on purpose.
Applying 'many mansions' (a promise about heaven) to the Church's schools is presented as a picture, with the heavenly meaning named first. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with the image.
'Not a hotel of strangers' is an image, not a claim.
